Rise for Impact

Founder and Team Lead of a youth initiative — and the person who builds its software.

Live

TypeScriptReactNext.jsVercelCI/CD
riseforimpact.org ↗Source ↗

Problem

Programmes run in four countries, and the people running them day to day are volunteers, not operators. Every routine change — publishing an update, opening applications, tracking a cohort — was a request that had to reach the one person who could deploy.

That is a bottleneck that gets worse as the organisation grows, and it is a technical problem dressed as an operations problem.

My role

I founded Rise for Impact in April 2025 and lead the team. I am also the only engineer on it, which means the roadmap and the implementation are decided by the same person — useful for speed, and something I have had to actively guard against when the convenient technical answer is not the right programme answer.

What I built

  • The public site and the application behind it, from schema through API to interface.
  • A content area programme staff publish through directly, without a deploy.
  • Fellowship application handling, from submission through review.
  • Admin tooling for tracking programmes across the four countries.
  • The deployment pipeline — GitHub to Vercel, with a preview build per branch so changes are reviewable before they go live.

Why these decisions

  • Volunteer-operable or it does not ship. Anything that required a developer to change was treated as a design failure. That is the single constraint that shaped the build, and it is why the content area exists at all.
  • A flat content model. Kept deliberately flat rather than nested, specifically to avoid the request waterfalls a nested model would have created on mobile data.
  • Preview build per branch. With one engineer there is no reviewer, so the preview deploy is the review step — it is the only thing standing between a bad change and the live site.

Most people arrive on mid-range Android devices over mobile data. Page weight and round trips mattered more than framework choice.

How I tested it

Honestly: there is no automated test suite on this project. Changes are verified through the per-branch preview deploy and manual checks before merge.

That is a real gap and I am naming it rather than implying coverage that does not exist. It is also the clearest difference between this project and Mboa Health, where the test gate came first — the contrast is mostly about what a solo founder chooses to spend the next hour on when a programme deadline is the binding constraint.

Evidence

  • The platform is live and publicly reachable at riseforimpact.org.
  • The stack is externally checkable: the live site serves images through Next.js image optimisation.
  • The repository is public, with 107 commits at last check.
  • The organisation publishes its own programme figures: 500+ young people engaged across programmes in 2025, four active countries, four university chapters, 600+ documented members.

Those are programme reach, published by the organisation — not platform accounts, not monthly actives. I have kept the distinction because conflating the two is the most common way a number like this becomes untrue.

Limitations and trade-offs

  • No automated tests, as above.
  • A bus factor of one. Every part of this system is understood by a single person, which is the largest risk the project carries and is not solved by documentation alone.
  • Founder and engineer being the same person removes the useful friction of having to justify a technical decision to someone else.
  • I have no platform analytics I am willing to publish, so I do not claim user numbers — only the programme figures the organisation itself publishes.

Current status

Live and in use. Programmes continue in Cameroon, Ghana, Nigeria and Rwanda.
